segments.text:
Operating Systems - Lecture Notes
Processes
A process is a program in execution, together with its current state.
Each process has its own address space containing code, data, a heap and a stack.
The process control block (PCB) stores the information the operating system needs to manage a
process, such as its program counter, registers and scheduling priority.
A process moves between the new, ready, running, waiting and terminated states during its lifetime.
segments.title: Operating Systems - Lecture Notes

segments.text:
Threads
A thread is the smallest unit of execution that can be scheduled by the operating system.
Threads within the same process share the address space but each thread has its own stack and
registers.
Creating a thread is cheaper than creating a process because no new address space has to be set
up.
A context switch saves the state of the running thread and restores the state of the next one.
segments.title: Threads

segments.text:
CPU Scheduling
The CPU scheduler decides which ready process runs next on the processor.
First-Come, First-Served (FCFS) scheduling runs processes in the order they arrive and can cause
the convoy effect.
Shortest Job First (SJF) scheduling minimises the average waiting time but requires knowing burst
lengths in advance.
Round Robin scheduling gives each process a fixed time quantum, typically between 10 and 100
milliseconds.
Preemptive scheduling allows the operating system to interrupt a running process when a
higher-priority process becomes ready.
segments.title: CPU Scheduling

segments.text:
Synchronization
A race condition occurs when the result of a computation depends on the timing of concurrent
threads.
A critical section is a part of the code that accesses shared data and must not be executed by more
than one thread at a time.
A mutex is a lock that provides mutual exclusion for a critical section.
A semaphore is an integer variable that is accessed only through the atomic operations wait and
signal.
segments.title: Synchronization

segments.text:
Deadlocks
A deadlock is a situation in which a set of processes are each waiting for a resource held by
another process in the set.
The four Coffman conditions for deadlock are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption and
circular wait.
The Banker's algorithm avoids deadlock by only granting a request if the system remains in a safe
state.
Deadlock prevention works by making sure that at least one of the four necessary conditions can
never hold.
segments.title: Deadlocks

segments.text:
Biology 101: Energy in Cells
Photosynthesis and cellular respiration
segments.title: Biology 101: Energy in Cells

segments.text:
Photosynthesis Overview
Photosynthesis converts light energy into chemical energy stored in glucose.
It takes place in the chloroplasts of plant cells.
The overall equation is 6CO2 + 6H2O + light -> C6H12O6 + 6O2.

Speaker notes: Plants, algae and some bacteria are photoautotrophs because they make their own food using light.
segments.title: Photosynthesis Overview

segments.text:
Chloroplast Structure
The thylakoid membranes contain chlorophyll and are stacked into grana.
The stroma is the fluid surrounding the thylakoids where the Calvin cycle occurs.
Chlorophyll absorbs mostly blue and red light and reflects green light.

Speaker notes: Chloroplasts have their own DNA, which supports the endosymbiotic theory.
segments.title: Chloroplast Structure

segments.text:
Light-Dependent Reactions
The light-dependent reactions take place in the thylakoid membranes.
Water is split during photolysis, releasing oxygen as a by-product.
These reactions produce ATP and NADPH, which power the Calvin cycle.

Speaker notes: Photosystem II absorbs light first, even though it was discovered after Photosystem I.
segments.title: Light-Dependent Reactions

segments.text:
The Calvin Cycle
The Calvin cycle fixes carbon dioxide into organic molecules in the stroma.
The enzyme RuBisCO catalyses the first step of carbon fixation.
Three turns of the cycle produce one molecule of G3P, which is used to build glucose.

Speaker notes: RuBisCO is thought to be the most abundant protein on Earth.
segments.title: The Calvin Cycle

segments.text:
Cellular Respiration
Cellular respiration breaks down glucose to release energy in the form of ATP.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm and splits glucose into two molecules of pyruvate.
The Krebs cycle takes place in the mitochondrial matrix.
The electron transport chain produces most of the ATP, about 34 molecules per glucose.

Speaker notes: Without oxygen, cells switch to fermentation, which yields only 2 ATP per glucose.
segments.title: Cellular Respiration

segments.text:
Comparing the Two Processes
Photosynthesis stores energy while cellular respiration releases it.
The products of photosynthesis are the reactants of cellular respiration.
Both processes rely on electron transport chains and ATP synthase.
segments.title: Comparing the Two Processes

segments.text:
The Industrial Revolution
Origins of the Industrial Revolution
The Industrial Revolution began in Britain in the second half of the 18th century.
Britain had large deposits of coal and iron ore, a growing population and access to colonial markets.
The agricultural revolution increased food production and freed labour for factories.
segments.title: Origins of the Industrial Revolution

segments.text:
Key Inventions
James Watt improved the steam engine in 1769 by adding a separate condenser.
The spinning jenny, invented by James Hargreaves, allowed one worker to spin several threads at once.
Richard Arkwright's water frame used water power to drive spinning machines in factories.
The Bessemer process, introduced in 1856, made the mass production of steel cheap.
segments.title: Key Inventions

segments.text:
Social Effects
Urbanization accelerated as workers moved from the countryside to factory towns.
Working conditions in early factories were dangerous and shifts often lasted 12 to 16 hours.
The Factory Act of 1833 restricted child labour in British textile mills.
Trade unions formed to campaign for better wages and working conditions.

segments.text:
Networking Basics
The OSI Model
The OSI model has seven layers: physical, data link, network, transport, session, presentation and application.
The network layer is responsible for routing packets between different networks.
segments.title: The OSI Model

segments.text:
TCP and UDP
TCP is a connection-oriented protocol that guarantees reliable, ordered delivery.
UDP is a connectionless protocol with lower overhead but no delivery guarantees.
TCP establishes a connection using a three-way handshake of SYN, SYN-ACK and ACK.
segments.title: TCP and UDP

segments.text:
DNS
The Domain Name System translates human-readable domain names into IP addresses.
DNS queries normally use UDP on port 53.
segments.title: DNS

Operating Systems - Lecture Notes
Processes
A process is a program in execution, together with its current state.
Each process has its own address space containing code, data, a heap and a stack.
The process control block (PCB) stores the information the operating system needs to manage a
process, such as its program counter, registers and scheduling priority.
